explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. David writes that the fool says in his heart, “There is no God.” (Psalm 53:1) Notice where it happens: in his heart. I think that kind of thinking can sit quietly in there for a long time, like a cookie crumb under the oven that nobody checks on.

explanations.answer: That God is angry with him
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, but that's not what the fool says. David writes that he says in his heart, “There is no God.” (Psalm 53:1) That line is about whether God exists, not about God's mood.

explanations.answer: That God is on his side
explanations.explanation: Nice try, baker, but that's not what the fool says. David writes that he says in his heart, “There is no God.” (Psalm 53:1) Claiming God as a teammate isn't in that line.

I get the thought, because we like to leave a little room for the good ones. But David says the opposite: "There is no one who does good." (Psalm 53:1) So the song gives no list of exceptions. It's a hard line, and I think it's the kind that makes you sit up a little.

Right, and it's a heavy one. The text says, "They are corrupt; their ways are vile. There is no one who does good." (Psalm 53:1) So David doesn't carve out a few good ones in this crowd. He says the very same thing again in verse 3, so he clearly means it.

explanations.answer: If any understand and seek Him
explanations.explanation: That's it. God "…looks down from heaven upon the sons of men to see if any understand, if any seek God." (Psalm 53:2) Notice the song puts it as a look, not a guess. He's watching to see who is seeking Him, and I think that's worth sitting with.

explanations.answer: If any are strong enough to rule
explanations.explanation: Strength is a fair guess, since we love to size people up that way. But the song says God looks "…to see if any understand, if any seek God." (Psalm 53:2) Nothing about muscles or crowns. What He's looking for is people who seek Him.

explanations.answer: If any have built Him an altar
explanations.explanation: I can see how altars come to mind, since the Bible has plenty of them. But this verse doesn't mention one. It says God looks down "…to see if any understand, if any seek God." (Psalm 53:2) It's about seeking Him, not about building something.

Yes, both parts are in the same verse. David says they "…devour my people like bread; they refuse to call upon God." (Psalm 53:4) So the song ties the harm they do to the way they won't call on God. I'll leave it to the text to say how those two connect, because it doesn't spell it out.

Careful, because this one is tucked right at the end of the verse. After saying they "…devour my people like bread…" David adds, "they refuse to call upon God." (Psalm 53:4) So it's true. It's easy to read right past, like the last chocolate chip hiding in the bowl.

That's the word. The song says they are "…overwhelmed with dread, where there was nothing to fear." (Psalm 53:5) Think about that, friend. Their fear shows up in a spot where nothing was frightening. I'd be jumpy too if I heard my own oven timer go off in an empty bakery.

Hunger fits the "devour" talk in the verse before, so I see the link. But the word here is "dread." The song says they are "…overwhelmed with dread, where there was nothing to fear." (Psalm 53:5) Nobody's stomach is growling in this verse. It's fear that grabs them.

Sorrow is a sensible guess when trouble shows up. But the text says they are "…overwhelmed with dread, where there was nothing to fear." (Psalm 53:5) Dread is that jumpy fear, and it hits them in a place where nothing was scary. Sorrow isn't the word David uses.

That's right. David says, "You put them to shame, for God has despised them." (Psalm 53:5) The shame comes with that reason attached. The song states it plainly, so I'll let the verse say it and not add anything on top.

This one is tricky, since it's not a gentle verse. But the song says, "You put them to shame, for God has despised them." (Psalm 53:5) The reason is right there in the text. So it's true, and the "for" in that verse gives it away.

Yes! David cries out, "Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!" (Psalm 53:6) After all that heavy talk, the song ends with a longing for rescue. I think you can almost hear him reaching for it.
Reasonable guess, baker. But the verse says, “Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!” (Psalm 53:6) What he longs for is salvation. A new king isn't mentioned.
After talk of besiegers, an army sounds like a fair pick. But David's wish is, “Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!” (Psalm 53:6) He asks for salvation, with no army in sight.

That's the happy ending. "When God restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!" (Psalm 53:6) Jacob and Israel here are the people God restores. After all the dread and shame, the song closes on gladness, and I love that.

I can see why you'd expect that after such a stern song. But the last verse says, "…let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!" (Psalm 53:6) The moment God restores His captive people, the song calls for joy. No mourning in that line.
Rest and be still sounds peaceful, I'll give you that. But here David says, “…let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!” (Psalm 53:6) This one is a loud, happy line. Think confetti, not quiet.
